variables.problem: Our cloud-gaming service renders frames in a data centre about 80 ms round trip from most players. Players feel their character answer the controller late, and quick aiming overshoots the target. We cannot move servers closer or cut the network delay further.
variables.tried: Lowering video bitrate and resolution to shave encode time.

rubric: A good idea borrows the predictive teleoperation design (76): predict the controlled agent's state locally on the user's side and periodically correct it with the authoritative remote state, so feedback appears without waiting for the round trip.

variables.problem: We route support tickets to 12 specialist teams with a learned router. Left alone it sent most tickets to three teams, so we forced an even split per batch. Now near-identical tickets land in different teams, and every team ends up learning the same common issues instead of specialising.
variables.tried: A per-batch quota that spreads tickets evenly across teams.

rubric: A good idea borrows similarity-preserving routing (56): a router loss that keeps the relational structure between inputs, so similar inputs get consistent assignments while load stays balanced.

variables.problem: We fine-tuned our code-review assistant only on review comments that human reviewers accepted. It now writes fluent, plausible comments, but it cannot tell a real bug from a style nitpick and ranks them the same way, because it never saw what a worse comment looks like.
variables.tried: More accepted comments; filtering short comments out of the training set.

rubric: A good idea borrows agentic critical training (84): train the model to pick the better of alternative actions (here, candidate comments) and reward that choice, instead of only imitating accepted outputs.

variables.problem: Our MRI protocol acquires every phase-encoding line of k-space, so a knee scan takes about 25 minutes and patients move, which blurs the image. We want to reconstruct diagnostic-quality images from only a fraction of the measurements.
variables.tried: Parallel imaging with more receiver coils.

rubric: A good idea borrows sparsity-constrained ghost imaging (89 or 88): reconstruct the image by optimisation with a sparsity prior from far fewer measurements than pixels.

variables.problem: Our learned order-execution agent occasionally sends orders that would breach the desk's exposure limits. When we added a large breach penalty to its training reward, it became timid and its execution quality dropped across the board. The limits are known exactly at decision time.
variables.tried: Reward shaping with a breach penalty; more training data from calm markets.

rubric: A good idea keeps the learned policy and adds an explicit check at decision time: the navigation challenge's learned planner with a geometric safety check layer (44), or a learned failure predictor that steers sampling away from failures (41).

variables.problem: Our 24-layer speech recogniser mis-transcribes accented speech. We cannot tell at which depth the representation of the accented audio goes wrong, so we do not know which layers to fine-tune or where to add adaptation.
variables.tried: Fine-tuning the whole model on accented data, which overfits.

rubric: A good idea borrows the layer-wise analysis of vision-language models (75): track output probabilities and feature representations across intermediate layers to find the critical layers where the representation changes.

variables.problem: We train a reinforcement-learning agent to schedule a hospital's operating rooms. Trained on full weekly schedules from the start, it almost never produces a feasible plan, so nearly every episode ends in the same failure penalty and it learns nothing.
variables.tried: Longer training; a denser hand-written reward.

rubric: A good idea borrows the curriculum used for sim-to-real navigation (40): start training on easy, small instances and raise difficulty as the agent succeeds, with a reward split into parts.

variables.problem: Our inspection drone fuses eight range sensors by averaging them with fixed weights. When one sensor is blocked or hit by glare, the fused distance is wrong. Which sensors to trust depends on the current readings themselves.

rubric: A good idea borrows attention (37, 38, 52 or 80): score each sensor's reading against a query built from the current context and fuse with the normalised scores as input-dependent weights.

variables.problem: Five teams each claim their pricing heuristic is the best. Their offline backtests use different data cuts and disagree with each other and with what we see in production, so every planning meeting reopens the argument.
variables.tried: Comparing each team's own backtest report.

rubric: A good idea borrows the cloth-unfolding benchmark's design (43): isolate the one decision step and run all candidates head to head under one standardised, live protocol.

variables.problem: Our search stack sends each query to the 3 best of 40 reranking models, picked by a small scoring network with a hard top-3 cut. The cut passes no gradient, so we train the scorer with a separate heuristic objective, and it keeps picking poor rerankers. We want the picker trained end to end with the rerankers.
variables.tried: A straight-through estimator; a softmax temperature schedule.

rubric: A good idea borrows ReMoE's fully differentiable router (53): replace the hard top-k selection with a continuous ReLU gate so a variable number of components is active and gradients reach the selector.

variables.problem: We train one predictive-maintenance model on two inputs at once: dense vibration sensor streams and short technician notes. Since adding the notes, accuracy on the sensor-only failure types dropped, and the two inputs seem to need very different amounts of model capacity and data.
variables.tried: Weighting the two losses; training on the notes first.

rubric: A good idea borrows the multimodal pretraining study's design (74): give each input type its own routing so capacity is allocated per modality instead of shared uniformly.

variables.problem: Our seismic survey needs a geophone every few metres to image the subsurface, and laying that many receivers in rough terrain is most of the survey's cost. We want comparable images from a much sparser receiver layout.

rubric: A good idea borrows sparsity-constrained ghost imaging (88 or 89): reconstruct the image by optimisation with a sparsity prior from far fewer measurements than the image has points.

variables.problem: Our handwriting-synthesis model generates pen trajectories in fixed-length chunks. The strokes look fine inside a chunk but jump or wobble where chunks meet, and it confuses the pen-down and pen-up phases of a letter.

rubric: A good idea borrows the assistive-robotics method (90): explicit phase tokens for the motion's stages plus overlapping chunk predictions blended to smooth the joins.
